title: After Always
subtitle: After Always · Chapter 40 of 40
content:
A year after Severus Snape was supposed to die, he complained about the quality of my handwriting on a grocery list.

It felt like victory.

Not the kind newspapers wrote about.

No banners. No speeches. No marble monument describing sacrifice in language the dead would have hated.

Just a Saturday morning at Spinner's End, rain tapping the kitchen window while Severus held the scrap of parchment at arm's length as if it had personally offended him.

“Is this ‘sage’?” he asked.

“Yes.”

“It resembles ‘rage.’”

“We already have that.”

His eyes lifted slowly.

I smiled into my tea.

The house had changed.

Not completely.

The narrow stairs still complained beneath heavy footsteps. The sitting room remained too dark because Severus claimed direct sunlight was hostile to books. The wallpaper in the upstairs hall was still ugly enough to qualify as a minor curse because neither of us could agree on a replacement.

But the kitchen walls were clean. The table no longer bore the word traitor carved into its surface. One cabinet held my mug beside his. A hook by the door carried two sets of laboratory robes. The new back windows looked into the potions annex, where morning light reflected from clean glass and brass fixtures.

There were signs of a future everywhere once I learned to recognize them.

A second toothbrush.

A stack of student essays Severus had not yet graded.

My notes on the antivenom paper we were preparing for publication.

A box of biscuits he pretended not to like.

A vase containing one crooked sprig of rosemary because he had discovered, to his irritation, that I enjoyed bringing bits of the garden indoors.

None of it was dramatic.

That was the point.

“What else?” he asked.

“Milk.”

He added it in precise script beneath my illegible version.

“Bread.”

“Already listed.”

“That's flour.”

He stared at the parchment.

I waited.

“Your handwriting is a public-health threat.”

“You're dating it.”

“I am dating you. The handwriting remains under review.”

He folded the list and put it in his pocket.

At noon, he had a Hogwarts seminar.

I went with him because we needed to collect moonstone from the laboratory stores and because, despite his protests, I enjoyed watching him teach now.

The castle no longer went silent when he entered.

People still noticed him. Some always would. Portraits whispered. Older students glanced twice. A visiting parent in the entrance hall recognized him and looked suddenly uncertain whether to offer a hand or back away.

Severus spared the man from deciding by walking past.

“Coward,” I murmured.

“Efficient.”

“Terrified of social interaction.”

“I spent years deceiving the most dangerous Legilimens alive.”

“And yet small talk defeats you.”

“Small talk has no strategic objective.”

I laughed as we descended toward the dungeons.

His class that day was brewing a modified Wiggenweld restorative.

The students were good. More importantly, they were unafraid to be wrong in front of him.

Severus still corrected them with surgical precision.

“Mr. Bell, if you pulverize the bark any further, you will have produced expensive dust.”

“Yes, Professor.”

“Miss Patel, the instruction says clockwise, not philosophically approximate clockwise.”

A few students snickered.

Patel rolled her eyes when his back was turned.

I saw it.

So did he.

He kept walking.

That might have been the greatest miracle of the entire post-war era.

Near the end of class, a cauldron began producing green vapor.

Three students moved before Severus spoke.

One killed the flame. One opened the vent. One stepped back and warned the neighboring table.

Severus watched them execute the safety procedure exactly as they had practiced.

The vapor cleared.

“What went wrong?” he asked.

Bell studied the ingredients. “The knotgrass was cut too early.”

“And why did no one get hurt?”

Patel answered this time.

“Because one mistake isn't supposed to become a catastrophe.”

Severus went still.

I remembered the first class.

So did he.

“Correct,” he said.

The word was quiet.

Afterward, while students packed their bags, Bell lingered.

“Professor?”

Severus looked up.

“My sister wants to do Potions next year. She's worried she's rubbish at it.”

“That is not a useful diagnostic category.”

Bell smiled nervously. “I know. I told her.”

Severus waited.

“Could I bring her my notes from the first unit?”

A year ago, I might have expected him to say that anyone needing borrowed notes lacked the discipline for advanced work.

Instead he opened a desk drawer.

“Take this.”

He handed Bell a thin packet.

It was a revised introductory guide Severus had written over the summer: measurement standards, common errors, safe substitutions, and a page titled WHAT TO DO WHEN YOU HAVE RUINED IT, which was considerably kinder than the title suggested.

Bell's face brightened.

“Thanks, Professor.”

“Return it unscorched.”

“I will.”

When the boy left, I leaned against Severus's desk.

“You made extra copies.”

“No.”

“There were six in the drawer.”

“Contingencies.”

“For anxious younger siblings?”

“For students inadequately prepared by previous instruction.”

“Mm-hm.”

His glare had lost much of its power over me.

Not all. I had standards.

We collected the moonstone and returned to Spinner's End before dusk.

The laboratory smelled faintly of dittany and clean metal. Our latest antivenom trial sat under stasis charms along the north bench. The paper beside it had two authors listed.

SEVERUS SNAPE.

And, beneath it, a blank line I could fill however I chose.

No forced name. No borrowed identity. Space without erasure.

Severus set the moonstone in storage and checked the ward ledger.

“Everything is accounted for,” he said.

“You sound disappointed.”

“I am relieved not to spend my evening searching for stolen toxic minerals.”

“Romantic plans?”

“I had considered dinner.”

“Scandalous.”

“And perhaps,” he continued, deliberately ignoring me, “an hour in which neither of us discusses anticoagulants.”

I put a hand to my chest. “Who are you?”

“Regretting this conversation.”

I came around the bench.

He watched me approach.

Even after a year, he never assumed touch.

Neither did I.

I lifted my hand.

He met it halfway.

His fingers were warm, stained faintly at the side with ink. The tremor that had once frightened both of us only appeared now when he was exhausted, and I had become very good at noticing exhaustion before he could turn it into an ethical principle.

“Dinner,” I agreed.

“Good.”

“No anticoagulants.”

“Preferably.”

“No Ministry correspondence.”

“Enthusiastically.”

“No grading.”

His expression became pained.

“Severus.”

“One essay.”

“No.”

“Half an essay.”

“That's not how essays work.”

“A paragraph.”

I kissed him.

It remained the most efficient method of negotiation I had discovered.

He responded with one hand settling at my waist and the other cupping the side of my face, careful around nothing because by now he knew I did not need to be handled like a fragile artifact. The kiss was warm, familiar, and still capable of turning every clever sentence in my head into useless sparks.

When we broke apart, he looked mildly annoyed by this effect despite being equally responsible for it.

“Manipulative,” he murmured.

“Effective.”

“Those are not synonyms.”

“Close enough.”

His thumb moved once along my cheek.

On the shelf behind him stood the old Advanced Potion-Making textbook.

We had not destroyed it.

We had also stopped treating it like scripture.

Some of Severus's corrections had been incorporated into the new safety guide, properly tested and cited. Some of the spells in the margins remained sealed under ward because brilliance did not make them harmless. The book was a record of a boy becoming dangerous and brilliant at the same time.

It was not the whole man.

Above the desk hung no Order medal, no Ministry commendation, no newspaper clipping.

There was only the brass laboratory plaque.

SPINNER'S END POTIONS LABORATORY
S. SNAPE & PARTNER

The second line had been his amendment.

The first time I saw it mounted, I had asked whether “partner” meant professional or romantic.

“Yes,” he had said.

I still liked the answer.

That evening we ate at the kitchen table while rain thickened against the windows.

Severus complained about the grocer's dried thyme. I complained about his insistence that knives had one objectively correct drawer. He read half a paragraph of a student's essay until I took it away from him. He retaliated by stealing the last potato from my plate.

After dinner, I found him standing by the sitting-room window.

His face had gone distant.

Not gone, exactly.

Some days the past still walked close enough to cast a shadow.

I joined him without speaking.

After a minute, he said, “Today is the nineteenth.”

I knew what he meant.

A year.

A year since the battle.

A year since the shack.

A year since he had expected the world to continue without him.

I reached for his hand.

He gave it to me.

“I used to think survival required justification,” he said.

I stayed quiet.

“That if I lived when others did not, I was obliged to convert every remaining hour into repayment.”

His fingers tightened around mine.

“I am beginning to suspect this was vanity.”

“Vanity?”

“The assumption that my suffering possessed sufficient value to balance a ledger.”

I turned toward him.

He gave a humorless little breath.

“Dumbledore would have enjoyed that sentence.”

“Probably.”

“I find that irritating.”

“Also probably.”

His eyes met mine.

“I do not know what to call this.”

“What?”

He gestured faintly: the house, the laboratory, the evening, me.

“A life?”

“That seems offensively simple.”

“Most true things are annoying like that.”

He looked out at the wet street again.

Once, one word had held an entire history for him.

Always.

People had turned it into a slogan because slogans were easier than contradictions. Easier than a boy who loved badly, a man who chose terribly, a spy who risked everything, a teacher who caused harm, a protector who saved children, a grieving person who confused punishment with devotion.

I did not ask him to stop remembering.

I did not ask him to replace the word.

I only stood beside him long enough for it to become something other than the last page.

Severus looked down at our hands.

“Tomorrow,” he said.

It was not a grand declaration.

That was why I loved it.

“Tomorrow,” I agreed.

He kissed my temple.

Behind us, the kettle began to whistle.

Neither of us moved immediately.

For once, there was no emergency in the sound.

No summons. No coded message. No poison boiling over. No war waiting on the other side of a door.

Just water becoming hot enough for tea.

Eventually Severus sighed.

“You'll let it boil dry.”

“You're closer.”

“This is your conception of partnership?”

“Yes.”

“Appalling.”

He went to the stove anyway.

I watched him, smiling.

The future did not arrive clean.

It arrived carrying scars, difficult memories, badly folded grocery lists, student essays, unfinished research, old grief, new habits, and more ordinary mornings than either of us had once believed we deserved.

It arrived because we kept choosing it.

Not once.

Not perfectly.

Again and again.

And when Severus handed me a cup of tea, his fingers brushing mine, I took it.

That was enough.

More than enough.

It was after always.

prose_fingerprint: emotionally direct without flattening emotion into exposition
ground abstract feelings in concrete physical details, objects, weather, rooms, gestures, and sensory anchors
alternate compact emotional beats with fuller reflective paragraphs
let dialogue carry relationship pressure while narration carries interior consequence
use humor and ordinary practical actions to make vulnerable scenes feel lived-in rather than staged
favor character-specific reactions and small remembered details over generic declarations
allow grief, identity, survival, belonging, home, change, vulnerability, care, and autonomy to recur as thematic pressure
end scenes or chapters on an emotional consequence, changed understanding, concrete image, callback, or forward pull
preserve first-person immediacy and avoid omniscient knowledge outside Jasper's perception
use semicolons selectively for linked thoughts rather than mechanically
dialogue_fingerprint: continuous dialogue should sound conversational rather than like alternating speeches
interrupt dialogue with gestures, environment, hesitation, humor, and internal reaction
let characters dodge, misunderstand, tease, repair, and return to earlier wording
do not make every character equally eloquent, equally dominant, or equally emotionally transparent
relationship_fingerprint: slow burn must accumulate evidence: remembered preferences, repaired conflict, shared routines, private jokes, and practical care
attraction should not erase plot, outside obligations, individual goals, or conflict
vulnerability is strongest when it changes later behavior
after an intense/private interlude, resume with reconnection, humor, care, consequences, memory updates, and the next plot beat rather than treating intimacy as a reset
